case_studies.title: Causal methods for LLM development and evaluation
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) development is currently driven by large-scale empirical iteration over data mixtures, reward models, routing strategies, and evaluation pipelines. Here, we argue that many central questions in LLM development and evaluation are inherently causal: What is the effect of adding a data domain during pretraining? How do annotator preferences change when LLMs generate text in a different style? Should a prompt be routed to a larger or smaller model given inference cost constraints? In general, causal methods are well-suited to such settings where interventions change outc
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of developing and evaluating large language models by using causal methods to understand the effects of changes in data, models, and prompts. The authors built a framework to apply causal methods to large language model development and evaluation. The result is a more effective way to develop and evaluate large language models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI or machine learning infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current large language model development and evaluation pipelines, consider applying causal methods to improve your models, and evaluate the potential benefits of using causal methods in your existing workflows.
case_studies.score_reasoning: High score due to relevance of LLMs, potential application in IT infrastructure, and value to IT engineers. Real-world impact is moderate due to novelty of approach, whereas AI maturity and monetization potential are more significant.

case_studies.abstract: AI-native software development is often evaluated at the level of individual models, prompts, or generated artifacts. This framing is insufficient for production environments where software must be continuously produced, verified, deployed, maintained, and adapted across many operational contexts and long time horizons. The result is a more robust and reliable software production architecture. This is relevant to IT work as it improves the deployment and maintenance of AI-native software.

case_studies.title: When Agents Control Robots: A Zero Trust Policy Model for Agentic Cyber-Physical Systems
case_studies.abstract: Multi-agent systems powered by large foundation models (LFMs) are increasingly deployed to control industrial robots through natural language, creating deployments in which security failures produce physical consequences. We analyse this threat landscape through Cobot-Claw, a deployed four-agent system for UR3e robotic arm control, and identify five attack classes specific to agentic cyber-physical systems. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of security risks in multi-agent systems controlling industrial robots, by building a Zero Trust Policy Model called ZTPM. The result is a framework that can prevent security failures with physical consequences. This research aims to mitigate risks in cyber-physical systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage industrial robot control systems using multi-agent systems, here is what to do: review your current security policies, assess the risk of physical consequences from security failures, and consider implementing a Zero Trust Policy Model like ZTPM to enforce security policies across all agents.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper on a real-world agentic system with security threat analysis and a proposed Zero Trust Policy Model, relevant to IT infrastructure and security.

case_studies.title: CelerLog: Fast Log Parsing via Dynamic Routing
case_studies.abstract: Log parsing is a fundamental step for automated log analysis, which transforms raw log messages into structured formats. Existing syntax-based parsers struggle with complex logs because they lack semantic reasoning ability. Emerging LLM-powered semantic parsers achieve high accuracy but suffer from prohibitive latency and token costs because they apply semantic inference across all logs. Our key observation is that not all logs necessitate complex semantic understanding: a vast majority of logs exhibit repetitive patterns that can be extracted via straightforward statistical analysis. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of slow log parsing by building a system called CelerLog, which uses dynamic routing to speed up the process. CelerLog achieves faster log parsing by applying semantic inference only when necessary, reducing latency and costs. The result is a more efficient log analysis system.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage log analysis systems, here is what to do: review your current log parsing method, consider implementing a dynamic routing approach like CelerLog, and assess potential latency and cost reductions. This flags a risk: if your org uses LLM-powered semantic parsers, check for potential performance bottlenecks immediately.
case_studies.score_reasoning: IT engineers could theoretically use LLM-powered logging parsers in Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace to optimize log analysis, but this paper focuses on log processing, not deployment. Novel application of LLMs in a non-agentic system, but relevant to IT infrastructure management. Low value within 90 days as it depends on specific tooling and implementation.

case_studies.title: L2IR: Revealing Latent Intent in Graph Fraud Detection
case_studies.abstract: Graph fraud detection has long depended on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to propagate and aggregate information across relational data. A critical obstacle in practice, however, is that fraudsters frequently disguise themselves by forging numerous connections with benign users, causing fraud signals to be progressively diluted during neighborhood aggregation and undermining detection reliability. While recent efforts have used Large Language Models (LLMs) to provide rich semantic cues for fraud detection, the underlying intent behind suspicious connections remains insufficiently explored. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of detecting latent intent in graph fraud by building a model called L2IR, which uses Large Language Models to improve detection reliability. The result is a more effective way to identify fraudsters who disguise themselves by forging connections with benign users. This affects IT work related to cloud infrastructure security and fraud detection.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure security, here is what to do: review your current fraud detection models, check if they use Graph Neural Networks, and consider integrating Large Language Models to improve detection reliability. This flags a risk: if your org uses GNNs for fraud detection, check for potential vulnerabilities in neighborhood aggregation immediately. Consider applying L2IR to strengthen your fraud detection capabilities.

case_studies.title: OrpQuant: Geometric Orthogonal Residual Projection for Multiplier-Free Power-of-Two Transformer Quantization
case_studies.abstract: The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) on edge devices is significantly constrained by memory limitations and the critical timing bottlenecks introduced by dense Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) arrays. In the ultra-low bit regime, logarithmic Power-of-Two (PoT) quantization provides a hardware-efficient alternative by replacing MAC operations with bit-shifts. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of memory limitations and timing bottlenecks in Large Language Models and Vision Transformers on edge devices by building a geometric orthogonal residual projection method for power-of-two transformer quantization, resulting in improved performance. The method replaces multiply-accumulate operations with bit-shifts, making it more hardware-efficient. This research may be relevant for optimizing AI model deployment on edge devices.

case_studies.title: SafeCtrl-RL: Inference-Time Adaptive Behaviour Control for LLM Dialogue via RL-Driven Prompt Optimisation
case_studies.abstract: Ensuring safe and contextually appropriate behaviour in Large Language Models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge for real-world deployment. We present \textbf{SafeCtrl-RL}, an inference-time behavioural control framework that enables adaptive safety regulation without model retraining or parameter modification. The method formulates dialogue generation as a sequential decision process, where a reinforcement learning agent dynamically selects prompt adjustment strategies based on contextual feedback. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of ensuring safe and contextually appropriate behaviour in Large Language Models, by building a framework called SafeCtrl-RL that enables adaptive safety regulation without model retraining. The result is a method that allows unsafe behaviours to be suppressed through iterative refinement. This does not directly relate to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.summary: This research aims to improve code review efficiency by identifying the types of changes within a patch, such as renames or logic modifications, using large language models. The result is a more efficient code review process, but it's primarily relevant to software development rather than cloud infrastructure management.
